questions.text:
Let A be a priority queue for maintaining a set of elements. Suppose A is implemented using a max-heap data structure. The operation Extract-Max(A) extracts and deletes the maximum element from A. The operation Insert(A,key) inserts a new element key in A. The properties of a max-heap are preserved at the end of each of these operations.
When A contains n elements, which one of the following statements about the worst case running time of these two operations is TRUE?
questions.solution:
A heap of n elements has height about log n:
- Extract-Max: remove the root, move the last element to the root, and heapify down the height of the tree [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]O(\log n)[/latex].
- Insert: add at the end and bubble up to the root [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]O(\log n)[/latex].

Answer: Both run in O(log(n))

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Both Extract-Max(A) and Insert(A,key) run in O(1).
Both Extract-Max(A) and Insert(A,key) run in O(log(n)).
Extract-Max(A) runs in O(1) whereas Insert(A,key) runs in O(n).
Extract-Max(A) runs in O(1) whereas Insert(A,key) runs in O(log(n)).

questions.text:
An algorithm has to store several keys generated by an adversary in a hash table. The adversary is malicious who tries to maximize the number of collisions. Let [latex] k[/latex] be the number of keys, [latex] m[/latex] be the number of slots in the hash table, and [latex] k \gt m[/latex].
Which one of the following is the best hashing strategy to counteract the adversary?
questions.solution:
Any fixed hash function (division or multiplication) is known to the adversary, who can pick keys that all collide.

Universal hashing picks the hash function at random from a family at run time, so the adversary cannot predict it, and the expected number of collisions stays small.

Answer: Universal hashing method

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: Division method, i.e., use the hash function [latex]h(k) = k\;  mod \; m[/latex]

Multiplication method, i.e., use the hash function [latex] h(k) =  \left \lfloor m(kA -\left \lfloor kA \right \rfloor ) \right \rfloor[/latex], where
[latex]A[/latex] is a carefully chosen constant.
If [latex]k[/latex] is a prime number, use Division method. Otherwise, use Multiplication method

questions.text:
Let SLLdel be a function that deletes a node in a singly-linked list given a pointer to the node and a pointer to the head of the list. Similarly, let DLLdel be another function that deletes a node in a doubly-linked list given a pointer to the node and a pointer to the head of the list.
Let n denote the number of nodes in each of the linked lists. Which one of the following choices is TRUE about the worst-case time complexity of SLLdel and DLLdel?
questions.solution:
To delete a node we must update its predecessor's next pointer.

- Singly linked list: the predecessor is found only by walking from the head [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]O(n)[/latex].
- Doubly linked list: the node's prev pointer gives the predecessor directly [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] [latex]O(1)[/latex].

Answer: SLLdel is O(n) and DLLdel is O(1)

Click here for detail solution by gateoverflow
options: SLLdel is O(1) and DLLdel is O(n)
Both SLLdel and DLLdel are O(log(n))
Both SLLdel and DLLdel are O(1)
SLLdel is O(n) and DLLdel is O(1)

questions.text:
Which one of the following sequences when stored in an array at locations
A[1], . . . , A[10] forms a max-heap?
questions.solution:
Max-heap: every parent [latex]A[i]\ge[/latex] its children [latex]A[2i][/latex], [latex]A[2i+1][/latex].

- Option 1: A[3] = 10 has child A[6] = 14 False
- Option 2: 23 [latex]\ge[/latex] 17, 14; 17 [latex]\ge[/latex] 7, 13; 14 [latex]\ge[/latex] 10, 1; 7 [latex]\ge[/latex] 5, 6; 13 [latex]\ge[/latex] 12 True
- Option 3: A[5] = 13 has child A[10] = 15 False
- Option 4: A[4] = 1 has children 12, 7 False

Answer: 23, 17, 14, 7, 13, 10, 1, 5, 6, 12
